entries.b9f04990dc53084c946253327ac4f477f7323c14: <div sID="gen18548" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="Ezek.9" sID="Ezek.9"/> <div eID="gen18548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18549" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18550" type="x-p"/> The prophet had, in vision, seen the wickedness that was committed at Jerusalem, in the foregoing chapter, and we may be sure that it was not represented to him worse than really it was; now here follows, of course, a representation of their ruin approaching; for when sin goes before judgments come next. Here is, I. Preparation made of instruments that were to be employed in the destruction of the city, <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.1-Ezek.9.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. The removal of the Shechinah from the cherubim to the threshold of the temple, <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.3">ver. 3</reference>. III. Orders given to one of the persons employed, who is distinguished from the rest, for the marking of a remnant to be preserved from the common destruction, <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.3-Ezek.9.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. IV. The warrant signed for the execution of those that were not marked, and the execution begun accordingly, <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.5-Ezek.9.7">ver. 5-7</reference>. V. The prophet's intercession for the mitigation of the sentence, and a denial of any mitigation, the decree having now gone forth, <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.8-Ezek.9.10">ver. 8-10</reference>. VI. The report made by him that was to mark the pious remnant of what he had done in that matter, <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.11">ver. 11</reference>. And this shows a usual method of Providence in the government of the world.
entries.9e98d1fe734d1169c38d6df0964fc1f180819249: <div eID="gen18550" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18549" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Preparations to Destroy Jerusalem; The Righteous Marked for Salvation. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  593.)</title> <div sID="gen18551" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> He cried also in mine ears with a loud voice, saying, Cause them that have charge over the city to draw near, even every man <hi type="italic">with</hi> his destroying weapon in his hand. <hi type="super">2</hi> And, behold, six men came from the way of the higher gate, which lieth toward the north, and every man a slaughter weapon in his hand; and one man among them <hi type="italic">was</hi> clothed with linen, with a writer's inkhorn by his side: and they went in, and stood beside the brasen altar. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the glory of the God of Israel was gone up from the cherub, whereupon he was, to the threshold of the house. And he called to the man clothed with linen, which <hi type="italic">had</hi> the writer's inkhorn by his side; <hi type="super">4</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto him, Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and set a mark upon the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry for all the abominations that be done in the midst thereof. <div eID="gen18551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18552" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen18552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18553" type="x-p"/> I. The summons given to Jerusalem's destroyers to come forth and give their attendance. He that appeared to the prophet (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.2">ch. viii. 2</reference>), that had brought him to Jerusalem and had shown the wickedness that was done there, <hi type="italic">he cried, Cause those that have charge over the city to draw near</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.1">v. 1</reference>), or, as it might better be read, and nearer the original, <hi type="italic">Those that have charge over the city are drawing near.</hi> He had said (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.18">ch. viii. 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will deal in fury;</hi> now, says he to the prophet, thou shalt see who are to be employed as the instruments of my wrath. <hi type="italic">Appropinquaverunt visitationes civitatis—The visitations</hi> (or visitors) <hi type="italic">of the city are at hand.</hi> They would not <hi type="italic">know the day of their visitations</hi> in mercy, and now they are to be visited in wrath. Observe, 1. How the notice of this is given to the prophet: <hi type="italic">He cried it in my ears with a loud voice,</hi> which intimates the vehemency of him that spoke; when men are highly provoked, and threaten in anger, they speak aloud. Those that regard not the counsels God gives them in a still small voice shall be made to hear the threatenings, to hear and tremble. It denotes also the prophet's unwillingness to be told this: he was deaf on that ear, but there is no remedy, their sin will not admit an excuse and therefore their judgment will not admit a delay: "<hi type="italic">He cried it in my ears with a loud voice;</hi> he made me hear it, and I heard it with a sad heart." 2. What this notice is. There are those <hi type="italic">that have charge over the city</hi> to destroy it, not the Chaldean armies, they are to be indeed employed in this work, but they are not the visitors, they are only the servants, or tools rather. God's angels have received a charge now to lay that city waste, which they had long had a charge to protect and watch over. They are at hand, as destroying angels, as ministers of wrath, for <hi type="italic">every man has his destroying weapon in his hand,</hi> as the angel that kept the way of the tree of life with a flaming sword. Note, Those that have by sin made God their enemy have made the good angels their enemies too. These visitors are called and <hi type="italic">caused to draw near.</hi> Note, God has ministers of wrath always within call, always at command, invisible powers, by whom he accomplishes is purposes. The prophet is made to see this in vision, that he might with the greater assurance in his preaching denounce these judgments. God told it him with a loud voice, <hi type="italic">taught it him with a strong hand</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.11">Isa. viii. 11</reference>), that it might make the deeper impression upon him and that he might thus proclaim it in the people's ears. <div eID="gen18553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18554" type="x-p"/> II. Their appearance, upon this summons, is recorded. Immediately <hi type="italic">six men came</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.2">v. 2</reference>), one for each of the principal gates of Jerusalem. Two destroying angels were sent against Sodom, but six against Jerusalem; for Jerusalem's doom in the judgment will be thrice as heavy as that of Sodom. There is an angel watching at every gate to destroy, to bring in judgments from every quarter, and to take heed that none escape. One angel served to destroy the first-born of Egypt, and the camp of the Assyrians, but here are six. In the Revelation we find seven that were to <hi type="italic">pour out the vials of God's wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.16.1">Rev. xvi. 1</reference>. They came with every one <hi type="italic">a slaughter-weapon in his hand,</hi> prepared for the work to which they were called. The nations of which the king of Babylon's army was composed, which some reckon to be six, and the commanders of his army (of whom <hi type="italic">six</hi> are named as principal, <reference osisRef="Jer.39.3">Jer. xxxix. 3</reference>), may be called <hi type="italic">the slaughter-weapons</hi> in the hands of the angels. The angels are thoroughly furnished for every service. 1. Observe whence they came—<hi type="italic">from the way of the higher gate, which lies towards the north</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.2">v. 2</reference>), either because the Chaldeans came from the north (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.14">Jer. i. 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">Out of the north an evil shall break forth</hi>) or because the image of jealousy was set up <hi type="italic">at the door of the inner gate that looks towards the north,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.3">ch. viii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.5">5</reference>. At that gate of the temple the destroying angels entered, to show what it was that opened the door to them. Note, That way that sin lies judgments may be expected to come. 2. Observe where they placed themselves: <hi type="italic">They went in and stood beside the brazen altar,</hi> on which sacrifices were wont to be offered and atonement made. When they acted as destroyers they acted as sacrificers, not from any personal revenge or ill-will, but with a pure and sincere regard to the glory of God; for to his justice all they slew were offered up as victims. <hi type="italic">They stood by the altar,</hi> as it were to protect and vindicate that, and plead its righteous cause, and avenge the horrid profanation of it. At the altar they were to receive their commission to destroy, to intimate that the iniquity of Jerusalem, like that of Eli's house, was <hi type="italic">not to be purged by sacrifice.</hi> <div eID="gen18554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18555" type="x-p"/> III. The notice taken of one among the destroying angels distinguished in his habit from the rest, from whom some favour might be expected; it should seem he was not one of the six, but <hi type="italic">among them,</hi> to see that mercy was mixed with judgment, <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.2">v. 2</reference>. This <hi type="italic">man was clothed with linen,</hi> as the priests were, and he had a <hi type="italic">writer's inkhorn</hi> hanging at <hi type="italic">his side,</hi> as anciently attorneys and lawyers' clerks had, which he was to make use of, as the other six were to make use of their <hi type="italic">destroying weapons.</hi> Here the honours of the pen exceeded those of the sword, but he was the Lord of angels that made use of the <hi type="italic">writer's inkhorn;</hi> for it is generally agreed, among the best interpreters, that this man represented Christ as Mediator saving those that are his from the flaming sword of divine justice. He is our <hi type="italic">high priest,</hi> clothed with holiness, for that was signified by the <hi type="italic">fine linen,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.8">Rev. xix. 8</reference>. As prophet he wears the <hi type="italic">writer's inkhorn.</hi> The book of life is the Lamb's book. The great things of the law and gospel which God has written to us are of his writing; for it is the Spirit of Christ, in the writers of the scripture, that testifies to us, and the Bible is <hi type="italic">the revelation of Jesus Christ.</hi> Note, It is a matter of great comfort to all good Christians that, in the midst of the destroyers and the destructions that are abroad, there is a Mediator, a great high priest, who has an interest in heaven, and whom saints on earth have an interest in. <div eID="gen18555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18556" type="x-p"/> IV. The removal of the appearance of the divine glory from over the cherubim. Some think this was that usual display of the divine glory which was between the cherubim over the mercy seat, in the most holy place, that took leave of them now, and never returned; for it is supposed that it was not in the second temple. Others think it was that display of the divine glory which the prophet now saw over the cherubim in vision; and this is more probable, because this is called <hi type="italic">the glory of the God of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.4">ch. viii. 4</reference>), and this is it which he had now his eye upon; this was gone <hi type="italic">to the threshold of the house,</hi> as it were to call to the servants that attended without the door, to send them on their errand and give them their instructions. And the removal of this, as well as the former, might be significant of God's departure from them, and leaving them their house desolate; and when God goes all good goes, but he goes from none till they first drive him from them. He went at first no further than <hi type="italic">the threshold,</hi> that he might show how loth he was to depart, and might give them both time and encouragement to invite his return to them and his stay with them. Note, God's departures from a people are gradual, but gracious souls are soon aware of the first step he takes towards a remove. Ezekiel immediately observed that <hi type="italic">the glory of the God of Israel had gone up from the cherub:</hi> and what is a vision of angels if God be gone? <div eID="gen18556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18557" type="x-p"/> V. The charge given <hi type="italic">to the man clothed in linen</hi> to secure the pious remnant from the general desolation. We do not read that this Saviour was summoned and sent for, as the destroyers were; for he is always ready, <hi type="italic">appearing in the presence of God for us;</hi> and to him, as the most proper person, the care of those that are marked for salvation is committed, <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.4">v. 4</reference>. Now observe, 1. The distinguishing character of this remnant that is to be saved. They are such as <hi type="italic">sigh and cry,</hi> sigh in themselves, as men in pain and distress, cry to God in prayer, as men in earnest, because of <hi type="italic">all the abominations that</hi> are committed in Jerusalem. It was not only the idolatries they were guilty of, but all their other enormities, that were abominations to God. These pious few had witnessed against those abominations and had done what they could in their places to suppress them; but, finding all their attempts for the reformation of manners fruitless, they sat down, and <hi type="italic">sighted, and cried,</hi> wept in secret, and complained to God, because of the dishonour done to his name by their wickedness and the ruin it was bringing upon their church and nation. Note, It is not enough that we do not delight in the sins of others, and that we have not fellowship with them, but we must mourn for them, and lay them to heart; we must grieve for that which we cannot help, as those that hate sin for its own sake, and have a tender concern for the souls of others, as David (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.136">Ps. cxix. 136</reference>), and Lot, who <hi type="italic">vexed his righteous soul</hi> with the wicked conversation of his neighbours. The abominations committed in Jerusalem are to be in a special manner lamented, because they are in a particular manner offensive to God. 2. The distinguishing care taken of them. Orders are given to find those all out that are of such a pious public spirit: "<hi type="italic">Go through the midst of the city</hi> in quest of them, and though they are ever so much dispersed, and ever so closely hid from the fury of their persecutors, yet see that you discover them, <hi type="italic">and set a mark upon</hi> their <hi type="italic">foreheads,</hi>" (1.) To signify that God owns them for his, and he will confess them another day. A work of grace in the soul is to God <hi type="italic">a mark upon the forehead,</hi> which he will acknowledge as his mark, and by which <hi type="italic">he knows those that are his.</hi> (2.) To give to them who are thus marked an assurance of God's favour, that they may know it themselves; and the comfort of knowing it will be the most powerful support and cordial in calamitous times. Why should we perplex ourselves about this temporal life if we know by the mark that we have eternal life? (3.) To be a direction to the destroyers whom to pass by, as the blood upon the door-posts was an indication that that was an Israelite's house, and the first-born there must not be slain. Note, Those who keep themselves pure in times of common iniquity God will keep safe in times of common calamity. Those that distinguish themselves shall be distinguished; those that cry for other men's sins shall not need to cry for their own afflictions, for they shall be either delivered from them or comforted under them. God will set a mark upon his mourners, will book their sighs and bottle their tears. The <hi type="italic">sealing of the servants of God in their foreheads</hi> mentioned in <reference osisRef="Rev.7.3">Rev. vii. 3</reference> was the same token of the care God has of his own people which is related here; only this was to secure them from being destroyed, that from being seduced, which is equivalent.
entries.6737777f568c26efca4f23aa31ec1ef50cbb7c21: <div eID="gen18557" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Righteous Distinguished; The Prophet's Intercession. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 593.)</title> <div sID="gen18558" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> And to the others he said in mine hearing, Go ye after him through the city, and smite: let not your eye spare, neither have ye pity: <hi type="super">6</hi> Slay utterly old <hi type="italic">and</hi> young, both maids, and little children, and women: but come not near any man upon whom <hi type="italic">is</hi> the mark; and begin at my sanctuary. Then they began at the ancient men which <hi type="italic">were</hi> before the house. <hi type="super">7</hi> And he said unto them, Defile the house, and fill the courts with the slain: go ye forth. And they went forth, and slew in the city. <hi type="super">8</hi> And it came to pass, while they were slaying them, and I was left, that I fell upon my face, and cried, and said, Ah Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ! wilt thou destroy all the residue of Israel in thy pouring out of thy fury upon Jerusalem? <hi type="super">9</hi> Then said he unto me, The iniquity of the house of Israel and Judah <hi type="italic">is</hi> exceeding great, and the land is full of blood, and the city full of perverseness: for they say, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath forsaken the earth, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> seeth not. <hi type="super">10</hi> And as for me also, mine eye shall not spare, neither will I have pity, <hi type="italic">but</hi> I will recompense their way upon their head. <hi type="super">11</hi> And, behold, the man clothed with linen, which <hi type="italic">had</hi> the inkhorn by his side, reported the matter, saying, I have done as thou hast commanded me. <div eID="gen18558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18559" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen18559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18560" type="x-p"/> I. A command given to the destroyers to do execution according to their commission. <hi type="italic">They stood by the brazen altar,</hi> waiting for orders; and orders are here given them to cut off and destroy all that were either guilty of, or accessory to, the abominations of Jerusalem, and that did not <hi type="italic">sigh and cry</hi> for them. Note, When God has <hi type="italic">gathered his wheat into his garner</hi> nothing remains but to <hi type="italic">burn up the chaff,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.3.12">Matt. iii. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen18560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18561" type="x-p"/> 1. They are ordered to destroy all, (1.) Without exception. They must <hi type="italic">go through the city, and smite;</hi> they must <hi type="italic">slay utterly,</hi> slay to destruction, give them their death's wound. They must make no distinction of age or sex, but cut off <hi type="italic">old and young;</hi> neither the beauty of the virgins, nor the innocency of the babes, shall secure them. This was fulfilled in the death of multitudes by famine and pestilence, especially by the sword of the Chaldeans, as far as the military execution went. Sometimes even such bloody work as this has been God's work. But what an evil thing is sin, then, which provokes the God of infinite mercy to such severity! (2.) Without compassion: "<hi type="italic">Let not your eye spare, neither have you pity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.5">v. 5</reference>); you must not save any whom God has doomed to destruction, as Saul did Agag and the Amalekites, for that is <hi type="italic">doing the work of God deceitfully,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.48.10">Jer. xlviii. 10</reference>. None need to be more merciful than God is; and he had said (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.18">ch. viii. 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">My eye shall not spare, neither will I have pity.</hi>" Note, Those that live in sin, and hate to be reformed, will perish in sin, and deserve not to be pitied; for they might easily have prevented the ruin, and would not. <div eID="gen18561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18562" type="x-p"/> 2. They are warned not to do the least hurt to those that were marked for salvation: "<hi type="italic">Come not near any man upon whom is the mark;</hi> do not so much as threaten or frighten any of them; it is promised them that there shall no evil come nigh them, and therefore you must keep at a distance from them." The king of Babylon gave particular orders that Jeremiah should be protected. Baruch and Ebed-melech were secured, and, it is likely, others of Jeremiah's friends, for his sake. God had promised that <hi type="italic">it should go well with his remnant</hi> and they <hi type="italic">should be well treated</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.11">Jer. xv. 11</reference>); and we have reason to think that none of the mourning praying remnant fell by the sword of the Chaldeans, but that God found out some way or other to secure them all, as, in the last destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, the Christians were all secured in a city called <hi type="italic">Pella,</hi> and none of them perished with the unbelieving Jews. Note, None of those shall be lost whom God has marked for life and salvation; for the foundation of God stands sure. <div eID="gen18562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18563" type="x-p"/> 3. They are directed to <hi type="italic">begin at the sanctuary</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.6">v. 6</reference>), that sanctuary which, in the chapter before, he had seen the horrid profanation of; they must begin there because there the wickedness began which provoked God to send these judgments. The debaucheries of the priests were the poisoning of the springs, to which all the corruption of the streams was owing. The wickedness of the sanctuary was of all wickedness the most offensive to God, and therefore there the slaughter must begin: "<hi type="italic">Begin</hi> there, to try if the people will take warning by the judgments of God upon their priests, and will repent and reform; <hi type="italic">begin</hi> there, that all the world may see and know that the Lord, whose name is <hi type="italic">Jealous,</hi> is <hi type="italic">a jealous God,</hi> and hates sin most in those that are nearest to him." Note, When judgments are abroad they commonly <hi type="italic">begin at the house of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17">1 Pet. iv. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">You only have I known, and therefore I will punish you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Amos iii. 2</reference>. God's temple is a sanctuary, a refuge and protection for penitent sinners, but not for any that <hi type="italic">go on still in their trespasses;</hi> neither the sacredness of the place nor the eminency of their place in it will be their security. It should seem the destroyers made some difficulty of putting men to death in the temple, but God bids them not to hesitate at that, but (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.7">v. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">Defile the house, and fill the courts with slain.</hi> They will not be <hi type="italic">taken from the altar</hi> (as was appointed by the law, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.14">Exod. xxi. 14</reference>), but think to secure themselves by <hi type="italic">keeping hold of the horns of</hi> it, like Joab, and therefore, like him, let them <hi type="italic">die there,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.30-1Kgs.2.31">1 Kings ii. 30, 31</reference>. There the blood of one of God's prophets had been shed (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.35">Matt. xxiii. 35</reference>) and therefore let their blood be shed. Note, If the servants of God's house defile it with their idolatries, God will justly suffer the enemies of it to defile it with their violences, <reference osisRef="Ps.79.1">Ps. lxxix. 1</reference>. But these acts of necessary justice were really, whatever they were ceremonially, rather a purification than a pollution of the sanctuary; it was <hi type="italic">putting away evil from among them.</hi> 4. They are appointed to <hi type="italic">go forth into the city,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.6-Ezek.9.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. Note, Wherever sin has gone before judgement will follow after; and, though <hi type="italic">judgement begins at the house of God,</hi> yet it shall not end there. The holy city shall be no more a protection to the wicked people then the holy house was to the wicked priests. <div eID="gen18563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18564" type="x-p"/> II. Here is execution done accordingly. They observed their orders, and, 1. <hi type="italic">They began at the</hi> elders, <hi type="italic">the ancient men that were before the house,</hi> and slew them first, either those seventy ancients who worshipped idols in their chambers (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.12">ch. viii. 12</reference>) or those twenty-five who <hi type="italic">worshipped the sun between the porch and the altar,</hi> who might more properly be said to be <hi type="italic">before the house.</hi> Note, Ringleaders in sin may expect to be first met with by the judgments of God; and the sins of those who are in the most eminent and public stations call for the most exemplary punishments. 2. They proceeded to the common people: <hi type="italic">They went forth and slew in the city;</hi> for, when the decree has gone forth, there shall be no delay; if God begin, he will make an end. <div eID="gen18564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18565" type="x-p"/> III. Here is the prophet's intercession for a mitigation of the judgement, and a reprieve for some (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">While they were slaying them, and I was left, I fell upon my face.</hi> Observe here, 1. How sensible the prophet was of God's mercy to him, in that he was spared when so many round about him were cut off. <hi type="italic">Thousands fell on his right hand, and on his left,</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">the destruction</hi> did <hi type="italic">not come nigh him; only with his eyes did he behold the just reward of the wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.91.7-Ps.91.8">Ps. xci. 7, 8</reference>. He speaks as one that narrowly escaped the destruction, attributing it to God's goodness, not his own deserts. Note, The best saints must acknowledge themselves indebted to sparing mercy that they are not consumed. And when desolating judgments are abroad, and multitudes fall by them, it ought to be accounted a great favor if we have our <hi type="italic">lives given us for a prey;</hi> for we might justly have perished with those that perished. 2. Observe how he improved this mercy; he looked upon it that <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he was left that he might stand in the gap to turn away the wrath of God. Note, We must look upon it that for this reason we are spared, that we may do good in our places, may do good by our prayers. Ezekiel did not triumph in the slaughter he made, but his <hi type="italic">flesh trembled for the fear of God,</hi> (as David's, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.120">Ps. cxix. 120</reference>); he <hi type="italic">fell on</hi> his <hi type="italic">face, and cried,</hi> not in fear for himself (he was one of those that were marked), but in compassion to his fellow-creatures. Those that sigh and cry for the sins of sinners cannot but sigh and cry for their miseries too; yet the day is coming when all this concern will be entirely swallowed up in a full satisfaction in this, that God is glorified; and those that now <hi type="italic">fall on their faces, and cry, Ah! Lord God,</hi> will lift up their heads, and sing, <hi type="italic">Hallelujah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.1">Rev. xix. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.3">3</reference>. The prophet humbly expostulates with God: "<hi type="italic">Wilt thou destroy all the residue of Israel,</hi> and shall there be none left but the few that are marked? Shall the Israel of God be destroyed, utterly destroyed? When there are but a few left shall those be cut off, who might have been the seed of another generation? And will the God of Israel be himself their destroyer? Wilt thou now destroy Israel, who wast wont to protect and deliver Israel? Wilt thou so <hi type="italic">pour out thy fury upon Jerusalem</hi> as by the total destruction of the city to ruin the whole country too? Surely thou wilt not!" Note, Though we acknowledge that <hi type="italic">God is righteous,</hi> yet we have leave to <hi type="italic">plead with him concerning his judgments,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.12.1">Jer. xii. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen18565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18566" type="x-p"/> IV. Here is God's denial of the prophet's request for a mitigation of the judgement and his justification of himself in that denial, <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.9-Ezek.9.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. 1. Nothing could be said in extenuation of this sin. God was willing to show mercy as the prophet could desire; he always is so. But here the case will not admit of it; it is such that mercy cannot be granted without wrong to justice; and it is not fit that one attribute of God should be glorified at the expense of another. Is it any pleasure to the Almighty that he should destroy, especially that he should destroy Israel? By no means. But the truth is their crimes are so flagrant that the reprieve of the sinners would be a connivance at the sin: "<hi type="italic">The iniquity of the house of Judah and Israel is exceedingly great;</hi> there is no suffering them to go on at this rate. <hi type="italic">The land is filled with the innocent blood,</hi> and, when the city courts are appealed to for the defence of injured innocency, the remedy is as bad as the disease, for <hi type="italic">the city is full of perverseness,</hi> or <hi type="italic">wrestling of judgement;</hi> and that which they support themselves with in this iniquity is the same atheistical profane principle with which they flattered themselves in their idolatry, <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.12">ch. viii. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Lord has forsaken the earth,</hi> and left it to us to do what we will in it; he will not intermeddle in the affairs of it; and, whatever wrong we do, he <hi type="italic">sees not;</hi> he either knows it not, or will not take cognizance of it." Now how can those expect benefit by the mercy of God who thus bid defiance to his justice? No; nothing can be offered by an advocate in excuse of the crimes while the criminal puts in such a plea as this in his own vindication; and therefore. 2. Nothing can be done to mitigate the sentence (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.10">v. 10</reference>): "Whatever thou thinkest of it, <hi type="italic">as for me, my eye shall not spare, neither will I have pity;</hi> I have borne with them as long as it was fit that such impudent sinners should be borne with; and therefore now <hi type="italic">I will recompense their way on their head.</hi>" Note, Sinners sink and perish under the weight of their own sins; it is their own way, which they deliberately chose rather than the way of God, and which they obstinately persisted in, in contempt of the word of God, that is <hi type="italic">recompensed on</hi> them. Great iniquities justify God in great severities; nay, he is ready to justify himself, as he does here to the prophet, for he will be <hi type="italic">clear when he judges.</hi> <div eID="gen18566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18567" type="x-p"/> V. Here is a return made of the writ of protection which was issued out for the securing of those that mourned in Zion (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">The man clothed with linen reported the matter,</hi> gave an account of what he had done in pursuance of his commission; he had found out all that mourned in secret for the sins of the land, and cried out against them by a public testimony, and had marked them all in the forehead. Lord, <hi type="italic">I have done as thou hast commanded me.</hi> We do not find that those who were commissioned to destroy reported what destruction they had made, but he who was appointed to protect reported his matter; for it would be more pleasing both to God and to the prophet to hear of those that were saved than of those that perished. Or this report was made now because the thing was finished, whereas the destroying work would be a work of time, and when it was brought to an end then the report should be made. See how faithful Christ is to the trust reposed in him. Is he commanded to secure eternal life to the chosen remnant? He has done as was commanded him. <hi type="italic">Of all that thou hast given me I have lost none.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ezek.9"/> <div eID="gen18567" type="x-p"/>

entries.cb8c89d233cadd6ac875bd917451dae541c3587e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11085"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 9</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.9.1-Ezek.9.11">Eze 9:1-11</reference>. Continuation of the Preceding Vision: The Sealing of the Faithful.</title> <div sID="gen19970" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11085"/><hi type="bold">1. cried--</hi>contrasted with their "cry" for mercy (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.18">Eze 8:18</reference>) is the "cry" here for vengeance, showing how vain was the former.<div eID="gen19970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19971" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them that have charge--</hi>literally, officers; so "officers" (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.17">Is 60:17</reference>), having the city in charge, not to guard, but to punish it. The angels who as "watchers" fulfil God's judgments (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.13">Da 4:13</reference>, 17, 23; <reference osisRef="Dan.10.20">10:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.21">21</reference>); the "princes" (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.3">Jr 39:3</reference>) of Nebuchadnezzar's army were under their guidance.<div eID="gen19971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19972" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">draw near--</hi>in the Hebrew intensive, "to draw near quickly." <div eID="gen19972" type="x-p"/>
entries.b34ac772e511629ecbdfbc46106e3cf5449c4dfe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11086"/><div sID="gen19973" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11086"/><hi type="bold">2. clothed with linen--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Dan.10.5">Da 10:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.6">12:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.7">7</reference>). His clothing marked his office as distinct from that of the six officers of vengeance; "linen" characterized the high priest (<reference osisRef="Lev.16.4">Le 16:4</reference>); emblematic of purity. The same garment is assigned to the angel of the Lord (for whom Michael is but another name) by the contemporary prophet Daniel (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.5">Da 10:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.6">12:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.7">7</reference>). Therefore the intercessory High Priest in heaven must be meant (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.12">Zec 1:12</reference>). The six with Him are His subordinates; therefore He is said to be "among them," literally, "in the midst of them," as their recognized Lord (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.6">He 1:6</reference>). He appears as a "man," implying His incarnation; as "one" (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.5">1Ti 2:5</reference>). Salvation is peculiarly assigned to Him, and so He bears the "inkhorn" in order to "mark" His elect (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.4">Eze 9:4</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Exod.12.7">Ex 12:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.3">Re 7:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.9.4">9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.16">13:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.4">20:4</reference>), and to write their names in His book of life (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.8">Re 13:8</reference>). As Oriental scribes suspend their inkhorn at their side in the present day, and as a "scribe of the host is found in Assyrian inscriptions accompanying the host" to number the heads of the slain, so He stands ready for the work before Him. "The higher gate" was probably where now the gate of Damascus is. The six with Him make up the sacred and perfect number, seven (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.9">Zec 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.5.6">Re 5:6</reference>). The executors of judgment on the wicked, in Scripture teaching, are good, not bad, angels; the bad have permitted to them the trial of the pious (<reference osisRef="Job.1.12">Job 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">2Co 12:7</reference>). The judgment is executed by Him (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.2">Eze 10:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.22">Joh 5:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.27">27</reference>) through the six (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.41">Mt 13:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.31">25:31</reference>); so beautifully does the Old Testament harmonize with the New Testament. The seven come "from the way of the north"; for it was there the idolatries were seen, and from the same quarter must proceed the judgment (Babylon lying northeast of Judea). So <reference osisRef="Matt.24.28">Mt 24:28</reference>.<div eID="gen19973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19974" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stood--</hi>the attitude of waiting reverently for Jehovah's commands.<div eID="gen19974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19975" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brazen altar--</hi>the altar of burnt offerings, not the altar of incense, which was of gold. They "stood" there to imply reverent obedience; for there God gave His answers to prayer [Calvin]; also as being about to slay victims to God's justice, they stand where sacrifices are usually slain [Grotius], (<reference osisRef="Ezek.39.17">Eze 39:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.34.6">Is 34:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.12.3">Jr 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.10">46:10</reference>). <div eID="gen19975" type="x-p"/>
entries.6afdcd0f6888a5a33f468827a3918aa30982e62a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11087"/><div sID="gen19976" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11087"/><hi type="bold">3. glory of ... God--</hi>which had heretofore, as a bright cloud, rested on the mercy seat between the cherubim in the holy of holies (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.2">2Sa 6:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.80.1">Psa 80:1</reference>); its departure was the presage of the temple being given up to ruin; its going from the inner sanctuary to the threshold without, towards the officers standing at the altar outside, was in order to give them the commission of vengeance. <div eID="gen19976" type="x-p"/>
entries.5331b9a1c3882d82a45389e9c5d9d715af4caf59: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11088"/><div sID="gen19977" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11088"/><hi type="bold">4. midst of ... city ... midst of Jerusalem--</hi>This twofold designation marks more emphatically the scene of the divine judgments.<div eID="gen19977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19978" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a mark--</hi>literally, the Hebrew letter Tau, the last in the alphabet, used as a mark ("my sign," <reference osisRef="Job.31.35">Job 31:35</reference>, Margin); literally, Tau; originally written in the form of a cross, which Tertullian explains as referring to the badge and only means of salvation, the cross of Christ. But nowhere in Scripture are the words which are now employed as names of letters used to denote the letters themselves or their figures [Vitringa]. The noun here is cognate to the verb, "mark a mark." So in <reference osisRef="Rev.7.3">Re 7:3</reference> no particular mark is specified. We seal what we wish to guard securely. When all things else on earth are confounded, God will secure His people from the common ruin. God gives the first charge as to their safety before He orders the punishment of the rest (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.20">Psa 31:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.20">Is 26:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">21</reference>). So in the case of Lot and Sodom (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.22">Ge 19:22</reference>); also the Egyptian first-born were not slain till Israel had time to sprinkle the blood-mark, ensuring their safety (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.7.3">Re 7:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.9">Am 9:9</reference>). So the early Christians had Pella provided as a refuge for them, before the destruction of Jerusalem.<div eID="gen19978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19979" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon the foreheads--</hi>the most conspicuous part of the person, to imply how their safety would be manifested to all (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.15.11">Jr 15:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.39.11-Jer.39.18">39:11-18</reference>). It was customary thus to mark worshippers (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.16">Re 13:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.1">14:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.9">9</reference>) and servants. So the Church of England marks the forehead with the sign of the cross in baptizing. At the exodus the mark was on the houses, for then it was families; here, it is on the foreheads, for it is individuals whose safety is guaranteed.<div eID="gen19979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sigh and ... cry--</hi>similarly sounding verbs in Hebrew, as in English Version, expressing the prolonged sound of their grief. "Sigh" implies their inward grief ("groanings which cannot be uttered," <reference osisRef="Rom.8.26">Ro 8:26</reference>); "cry," the outward expression of it. So Lot (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.7">2Pe 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>). Tenderness should characterize the man of God, not harsh sternness in opposing the ungodly (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.53">Psa 119:53</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.136">136</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.13.17">Jr 13:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.21">2Co 12:21</reference>); at the same time zeal for the honor of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.9">Psa 69:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.19">1Jo 5:19</reference>). <div eID="gen19980" type="x-p"/>
entries.96035b690cd5081a0101176888ca2bf201dfa51a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11089"/><div sID="gen19981" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11089"/><hi type="bold">5. the others--</hi>the six officers of judgment (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.2">Eze 9:2</reference>). <div eID="gen19981" type="x-p"/>
entries.2859860dac4f76ecd7f750d0c83d7c1fa7571b55: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11090"/><div sID="gen19982" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11090"/><hi type="bold">6. come not near any ... upon whom ... mark--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.9.4">Re 9:4</reference>). It may be objected that Daniel, Jeremiah, and others were carried away, whereas many of the vilest were left in the land. But God does not promise believers exemption from all suffering, but only from what will prove really and lastingly hurtful to them. His sparing the ungodly turns to their destruction and leaves them without excuse [Calvin]. However, the prophecy waits a fuller and final fulfilment, for <reference osisRef="Rev.7.3-Rev.7.8">Re 7:3-8</reference>, in ages long after Babylon, foretells, as still future, the same sealing of a remnant (one hundred forty-four thousand) of Israel previous to the final outpouring of wrath on the rest of the nation; the correspondence is exact; the same pouring of fire from the altar follows the marking of the remnant in both (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.8.5">Re 8:5</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.2">Eze 10:2</reference>). So <reference osisRef="Zech.13.9">Zec 13:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.2">14:2</reference>, distinguish the remnant from the rest of Israel.<div eID="gen19982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19983" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">begin at ... sanctuary--</hi>For in it the greatest abominations had been committed; it had lost the reality of consecration by the blood of victims sacrificed to idols; it must, therefore, lose its semblance by the dead bodies of the slain idolaters (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.7">Eze 9:7</reference>). God's heaviest wrath falls on those who have sinned against the highest privileges; these are made to feel it first (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17">1Pe 4:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.18">18</reference>). He hates sin most in those nearest to Him; for example, the priests, &c.<div eID="gen19983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19984" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ancient men--</hi>the seventy elders. <div eID="gen19984" type="x-p"/>
entries.683020aa9303f2d6e6f59221ab6d5cab4ac67f54: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11091"/><div sID="gen19985" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11091"/><hi type="bold">8. I was left--</hi>literally, "there was left I." So universal seemed the slaughter that Ezekiel thought himself the only one left [Calvin]. He was the only one left of the priests "in the sanctuary."<div eID="gen19985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19986" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fell upon my face--</hi>to intercede for his countrymen (so <reference osisRef="Num.16.22">Nu 16:22</reference>).<div eID="gen19986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19987" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all the residue--</hi>a plea drawn from God's covenant promise to save the elect remnant. <div eID="gen19987" type="x-p"/>
entries.3277243d44603522f4de5d835a40e990da02eee4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11092"/><div sID="gen19988" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11092"/><hi type="bold">9. exceeding--</hi>literally, "very, very"; doubled.<div eID="gen19988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19989" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perverseness--</hi>"apostasy" [Grotius]; or, "wresting aside of justice."<div eID="gen19989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19990" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord ... forsaken ... earth ... seeth not--</hi>The order is reversed from <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.12">Eze 8:12</reference>. There they speak of His neglect of His people in their misery; here they go farther and deny His providence (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.11">Psa 10:11</reference>), so that they may sin fearlessly. God, in answer to Ezekiel's question (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.8">Eze 9:8</reference>), leaves the difficulty unsolved; He merely vindicates His justice by showing it did not exceed their sin: He would have us humbly acquiesce in His judgments, and wait and trust. <div eID="gen19990" type="x-p"/>
entries.4d15945a0c209681be715c22d9b645440c1ed1b7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11093"/><div sID="gen19991" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11093"/><hi type="bold">10. mine eye--</hi>to show them their mistake in saying, "The Lord seeth not."<div eID="gen19991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19992" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">recompense their way upon their head--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.1.31">Pr 1:31</reference>). Retribution in kind. <div eID="gen19992" type="x-p"/>
entries.514a68096b7861f3e38e8d244d3d75d0f6be7787: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11094"/><div sID="gen19993" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11094"/><hi type="bold">11. I have done as thou hast commanded--</hi>The characteristic of Messiah (<reference osisRef="John.17.4">Joh 17:4</reference>). So the angels (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.21">Psa 103:21</reference>); and the apostles report their fulfilment of their orders (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.30">Mr 6:30</reference>). <chapter eID="Ezek.9"/>

entries.95959e6653bb692758017f3c5f1a1266b3849a5b: <div eID="gen31427" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31428" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31429" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31429" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31428" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31430" type="x-p"/> The vision in this chapter seems intended to denote the general destruction of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, excepting a few pious individuals that were distressed at the abominations that were committed in the land; who, in order to be delivered from the general calamity, were Marked, in allusion, perhaps, to the custom of eastern princes, who marked their servants in the forehead, or rather to the custom very frequent among the Pagan worshippers, of indelibly imprinting on different parts of their body the marks of their idols. To indicate, likewise, that God was soon to forsake the temple, the shechinah, or glorious symbol of his presence, is seen to remove from the inner sanctuary to the threshold or door of the temple, <reference osisRef="Eze.9.1-Eze.9.7">Eze 9:1-7</reference>. The prophet intercedes for his people; but God, on account of the greatness of their sins, will not be entreated, <reference osisRef="Eze.9.8-Eze.9.11">Eze 9:8-11</reference>. <div eID="gen31430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31431" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen31431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31432" type="x-p"/> Cause them that have charge over the city - By those six men with destroying weapons the Chaldeans are represented, who had received commission to destroy the city; and when the north is mentioned in such cases, Chaldea and the Chaldean armies are generally intended. There appears to have been six men with a sort of slaughter-bills, and one man with an inkhorn. These may represent the seven counsellors of the eastern monarchs, who always saw the king's face, and knew all the secrets of the government. One of them was that minister who had the office of reporting concerning criminals, who carried the book of death and the book of life into the presence of the king, where the names were entered of criminals who were destined to suffer, and of those who were either considered as innocent or recommended to mercy; those of the former in the book of death, those of the latter in the book of life. This person with the inkhorn might be termed, in our phrase, the recorder.
entries.5136cbb31b796139633a907c6a844b32106bc695: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen31432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31433" type="x-p"/> Stood beside the brazen altar - To signify that the people against whom they had their commission were, for their crimes, to be sacrificed to the demands of Divine justice.
entries.95426b54cda5b8c60473125008714f0d9b9ec589: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen31433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31434" type="x-p"/> And he called to the man - The person here who called was that who sat on the chariot of the Divine glory. See <reference osisRef="Eze.1.26">Eze 1:26</reference>.
entries.8e1806e862a54b9f1b3ab8f70fcc24f874a477f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen31434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31435" type="x-p"/> Set a mark upon the foreheads of the men that sigh - This is in allusion to the ancient every-where-used custom of setting marks on servants and slaves, to distinguish them from others. It was also common for the worshippers of particular idols to have their idol's mark upon their foreheads, arms, etc. These are called sectarian marks to the present day among the Hindoos and others in India. Hence by this mark we can easily know who is a follower of Vishnoo, who of Siva, who of Bramah, etc. The original words, והתוית תו vehithvitha tau, have been translated by the Vulgate, et signa thau, "and mark thou tau on the foreheads," etc. St. Jerome and many others have thought that the letter tau was that which was ordered to be placed on the foreheads of those mourners; and Jerome says, that this Hebrew letter ת tau was formerly written like a cross. So then the people were to be signed with the sign of the cross! It is certain that on the ancient Samaritan coins, which are yet extant, the letter ת tau is in the form +, which is what we term St. Andrew's cross. The sense derived from this by many commentators is, that God, having ordered those penitents to be marked with this figure, which is the sign of the cross, intimated that there is no redemption nor saving of life but by the cross of Christ, and that this will avail none but the real penitent. All this is true in itself, but it is not true in respect to this place. The Hebrew words signify literally, thou shalt make a mark, or sign a sign, but give no intimation what that mark or sign was. It was intended here to be what the sprinkling of the blood of the paschal lamb on the lintels and door-posts of the Israelites was, namely, a notice to the destroying angel what house he should spare. As the whole of this matter only passed in vision we are bound to neither letter, nor any other kind of figure. The symbolical action teaches us that God, in general judgments, will make a distinction between the innocent and the guilty, between the penitent and the hardened sinner.
entries.1685a708ddcadd6b593d0a24562645d83cf6acc1: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen31435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31436" type="x-p"/> Begin at my sanctuary - Let those who have sinned against most mercy, and most privileges, be the first victims of justice. Those who know their Lord's will, and do it not, shall be beaten with many stripes. The unfaithful members of Christ's church will be first visited and most punished. But let not those who belong to the synagogue of Satan exult in this, for if judgment begin at the house of God what will the end be of them who obey not the Gospel! However, the truly penitent of all descriptions in such cases shall be safe. The command of God is, "Set a mark on all them that sigh and cry;" and his command to the destroyers is, "Come not near any man on whom is the mark."
entries.2a368c4704b143769c945b99cb18cbc71f175f9b: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen31436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31437" type="x-p"/> Defile the house - A dreadful sentence, Let it be polluted, I will no more dwell in it; I now utterly forsake it.
entries.d6be0b63489e4c920357e022d923bc76682be383: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen31437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31438" type="x-p"/> Wilt thou destroy all the residue of Israel, On thy pouring out of thy fury upon Jerusalem? - These destroyers had slain the seventy elders, the twenty-five adorers of the sun, and the women that mourned for Tammuz; and on seeing this slaughter the prophet fell on his face, and began to make intercession.
entries.a0c00bf20ea2fa24e80df1cfea27d2e4a158a6a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen31438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31439" type="x-p"/> For they say, The Lords hath forsaken the earth - את הארץ eth haarets, "this land." He has no more place in Israel; he has quite abandoned it; he neither sees nor cares, and he can be no longer the object of worship to any man in Israel. This seems to be the meaning; and God highly resents it, because it was bringing him on a level with idols and provincial deities, who had, according to supposition, regency only in some one place.
entries.12bf1a34450a6a259af0c5664a276a3e5ccb1ba2: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen31439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31440" type="x-p"/> Mine eye shall not spare - They say, the Lord seeth not: this is false; I have seen all their iniquities, and do see all their abominations; and I will bring deserved judgment upon them, and then that eye which now sees will neither pity nor spare.
entries.ae8d0073646c40bd18ec4ea48d05aac8d9b2297c: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen31440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31441" type="x-p"/> I have done as thou hast commanded me - Angels and men must all give account of their conduct to God; for although he is every where, and his eye sees all things, yet they must personally account for all that they have done. I have done as thou hast commanded me. The penitents are all signed; the penitents are all safe. This is good news for them that mourn.  <chapter eID="Ezek.9"/> <div eID="gen31441" type="x-p"/>

entries.6d47667914d9381f53ed666c079573b4c8fe138c: <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.1-Ezek.9.3">Eze 9:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen14852" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Angels which Smite Jerusalem</title> <div sID="gen14853" type="x-p"/> At the call of Jehovah, His servants appear to execute the judgment. - Eze 9:1. <hi type="italic">And He called in my ears with a loud voice, saying, Come hither, ye watchmen of the city, and every one his instrument of destruction in his hand.</hi> Eze 9:2. <hi type="italic">And behold six men came by the way of the upper gage, which is directed toward the north, every one with his smashing-tool in his hand; and a man in the midst of them, clothed in white linen, and writing materials by his hip; and they came and stood near the brazen altar.</hi> Eze 9:3. <hi type="italic">And the glory of the God of Israel rose up from the cherub, upon which it was, to the threshold of the house, and called to the man clothed in white linen, by whose hip the writing materials were.</hi> -  פּקדּות העיר does not mean the punishments of the city. This rendering does not suit the context, since it is not the punishments that are introduced, but the men who execute them; and it is not established by the usage of the language. פּקדּה is frequently used, no doubt, in the sense of visitation or chastisement (e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.10.3">Isa 10:3</reference>; Hos 9:7); but it is not met with in the plural in this sense. In the plural it only occurs in the sense of supervision or protectorate, in which sense it occurs not only in <reference osisRef="Jer.52.11">Jer 52:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.11">Eze 44:11</reference>, but also (in the singular) in <reference osisRef="Isa.60.17">Isa 60:17</reference>, and as early as Num 3:38, where it relates to the presidency of the priests, and very frequently in the Chronicles. Consequently פּקדּות are those whom God has appointed to watch over the city, the city-guard (2Ki 11:18), - not earthly, but heavenly watchmen, - who are now to inflict punishment upon the ungodly, as the authorities appointed by God. קרבוּ is an imperative <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.41.21">Isa 41:21</reference>, and must not be altered into קרבוּ (<hi type="italic">Kal</hi>), as Hitzig proposes. The <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> is used in an intransitive sense, <hi type="italic">festinanter appropinquavit</hi>, as in Eze 36:8. The persons called come by the way of the upper northern gate of the temple, to take their stand before Jehovah, whose glory had appeared in the inner court. The upper gate is the gate leading from the outer court to the inner, or upper court, which stood on higher ground, - the gate mentioned in <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.3">Eze 8:3</reference> and Eze 8:5. In the midst of the six men furnished with smashing-tools there was one clothed in white byssus, with writing materials at his side. The dress and equipment, as well as the instructions which he afterwards receives and executes, show him to be the prince or leader of the others. <div eID="gen14853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14854" type="x-p"/> Kliefoth calls in question the opinion that these seven men are angels; but without any reason. Angels appearing in human form are frequently called אנשׁים or אישׁ, according to their external <hi type="italic">habitus</hi>. But the number seven neither presupposes the dogma of the seven archangels, nor is copied from the seven Parsic <hi type="italic">amschaspands</hi>. The dress worn by the high priest, when presenting the sin-offering on the great day of atonement (<reference osisRef="Lev.16.4">Lev 16:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.23">Lev 16:23</reference>), was made of בּד, i.e., of white material woven from byssus thread (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Exod.28.42">Exo 28:42</reference>). It has been inferred from this, that the figure clothed in white linen was the angel of Jehovah, who appears as the heavenly high priest, to protect and care for his own. In support of this, the circumstance may be also adduced, that the man whom Daniel saw above the water of the Tigris, and whose appearance is described, in <reference osisRef="Dan.10.5-Dan.10.6">Dan 10:5-6</reference>, in the same manner as that of Jehovah in <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.4">Eze 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.26-Ezek.1.27">Eze 1:26-27</reference>, and that of the risen Christ in <reference osisRef="Rev.1.13-Rev.1.15">Rev 1:13-15</reference>, appears clothed in בּדּים (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.5">Dan 10:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.6-Dan.12.7">Dan 12:6-7</reference>).<note placement="foot">לבוּשׁ בּדּים is rendered by the lxx, in the passage before us, ἐνδεδυκώς ποδήρῃ. It is in accordance with this that Christ is described in <reference osisRef="Rev.1.13">Rev 1:13</reference> as clothed with a ποδήρης, and not after <reference osisRef="Dan.10.5">Dan 10:5</reference>, as Hengstenberg supposes. In <reference osisRef="Dan.10.5">Dan 10:5</reference>, the Septuagint has ἐνδεδυμένος βαδδίν or τὰ βαδδίν. In other places, the Sept. rendering of בּד is λίνον (thus <reference osisRef="Lev.16.4">Lev 16:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.23">Lev 16:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.6.3">Lev 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.28.42">Exo 28:42</reference>, etc.); and hence the λίνον λαμπρόν of <reference osisRef="Rev.15.6">Rev 15:6</reference> answers to the בּד made of שׁשׁ, βύσσος, and is really the same as the βύσσινον λαμπρόν of Rev 19:8.</note> <div eID="gen14854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14855" type="x-p"/> Nevertheless, we cannot regard this view as established. The shining white talar, which is evidently meant by the plural בּדּים, occurring only here and in Daniel (<hi type="italic">ut. sup.</hi>), is not a dress peculiar to the angel of Jehovah or to Christ. The seven angels, with the vials of wrath, also appear in garments of shining white linen (ἐνδεδυμένοι λίνον καθαρὸν λαμπρόν, <reference osisRef="Rev.15.6">Rev 15:6</reference>); and the shining white colour, as a symbolical representation of divine holiness and glory (see comm. on <reference osisRef="Lev.16.4">Lev 16:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Rev.19.8">Rev 19:8</reference>), is the colour generally chosen for the clothing both of the heavenly spirits and of “just men made perfect” (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.8">Rev 19:8</reference>). Moreover, the angel with the writing materials here is described in a totally different manner from the appearance of Jehovah in Ezekiel 1 and Daniel 10, or that of Christ in Rev 1; ; and there is nothing whatever to indicate a being equal with God. Again, the distinction between him and the other six men leads to no other conclusion, than that he stood in the same relation to them as the high priest to the Levites, or the chancellor to the other officials. This position is indicated by the writing materials on his hips, i.e., in the girdle on his hips, in which scribes in the East are accustomed to carry their writing materials (vid., Rosenmüller, <hi type="italic">A. u. N. Morgenland</hi>, IV. p. 323). He is provided with these for the execution of the commission given to him in Eze 9:4. In this way the description can be very simply explained, without the slightest necessity for our resorting to Babylonian representations of the god Nebo, i.e., Mercury, as the scribe of heaven. The seven men take their station by the altar of burnt-offering, because the glory of God, whose commands they were about to receive, had taken up its position there for the moment (Kliefoth); not because the apostate priesthood was stationed there (Hävernick). The glory of Jehovah, however, rose up from the cherub to the threshold of the house. The meaning of this is not that it removed from the interior of the sanctuary to the outer threshold of the temple-building (Hävernick), for it was already stationed, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.16">Eze 8:16</reference>, above the cherub, between the porch and the altar. It went back from thence to the threshold of the temple-porch, through which one entered the Holy Place, to give its orders there. The reason for leaving its place above the cherubim (the singular כּרוּב is used collectively) to do this, was not that “God would have had to turn round in order to address the seven from the throne, since, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.4">Eze 8:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.16">Eze 8:16</reference>, He had gone from the north gate of the outer court into the inner court, and His servants had followed Him” (Hitzig); for the cherubim moved in all four directions, and therefore God, even from the throne, could turn without difficulty to every side. God left His throne, that He might issue His command for the judgment upon Israel from the threshold of the temple, and show Himself to be the judge who would forsake the throne which He had assumed in Israel. This command He issues from the temple court, because the temple was the place whence God attested Himself to His people, both by mercy and judgment.
entries.83406b16cc140205bd3756245d90566cf4b9394f: <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.4-Ezek.9.7">Eze 9:4-7</reference> <div eID="gen14855" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Divine Command</title> <div sID="gen14856" type="x-p"/> Eze 9:4. <hi type="italic">And Jehovah said to him, Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and mark a cross upon the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations which take place in their midst.</hi> Eze 9:5. <hi type="italic">And to those he said in my ears: Go through the city behind him, and smite. Let not your eye look compassionately, and do not spare.</hi> Eze 9:6. <hi type="italic">Old men, young men, and maidens, and children, and women, slay to destruction: but ye shall not touch any one who has the cross upon him; and begin at my sanctuary. And they began with the old men, who were before the house.</hi> Eze 9:7. <hi type="italic">And He said to them, defile the house, and fill the courts with slain; go ye out. And they went out, and smote in the city.</hi> - God commands the man provided with the writing materials to mark on the forehead with a cross all the persons in Jerusalem who mourn over the abominations of the nation, in order that they may be spared in the time of the judgment. תּו, the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet, had the form of a cross in the earlier writing. התוה תּו, to mark a ת, is therefore the same as to make a mark in the form of a cross; although there was at first no other purpose in this sign than to enable the servants employed in inflicting the judgment of God to distinguish those who were so marked, so that they might do them no harm. Eze 9:6. And this was the reason why the תּו was to be marked upon the forehead, the most visible portion of the body; the early Christians, according to a statement in Origen, looked upon the sign itself as significant, and saw therein a prophetic allusion to the sign of the cross as the distinctive mark of Christians. A direct prophecy of the cross of Christ is certainly not to be found here, since the form of the letter <hi type="italic">Tâv</hi> was the one generally adopted as a sign, and, according to <reference osisRef="Job.31.35">Job 31:35</reference>, might supply the place of a signature. Nevertheless, as Schmieder has correctly observed, there is something remarkable in this coincidence to the thoughtful observer of the ways of God, whose counsel has carefully considered all before hand, especially when we bear in mind that in the counterpart to this passage (<reference osisRef="Rev.7.3">Rev 7:3</reference>) the seal of the living God is stamped upon the foreheads of the servants of God, who are to be exempted from the judgment, and that according to <reference osisRef="Rev.14.1">Rev 14:1</reference> they had the name of God written upon their foreheads. So much, at any rate, is perfectly obvious from this, namely, that the sign was not arbitrarily chosen, but was inwardly connected with the fact which it indicated; just as in the event upon which our vision is based (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.13">Exo 12:13</reference>, Exo 12:22.) the distinctive mark placed upon the houses of the Israelites in Egypt, in order that the destroying angel might pass them by, namely, the smearing of the doorposts with the blood of the paschal lamb that had been slain, was selected on account of its significance and its corresponding to the thing signified. The execution of this command is passed over as being self-evident; and it is not till <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.11">Eze 9:11</reference> that it is even indirectly referred to again. <div eID="gen14856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14857" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.5">Eze 9:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.6">Eze 9:6</reference> there follows, first of all, the command given to the other six men. They are to go through the city, behind the man clothed in white linen, and to smite without mercy all the inhabitants of whatever age or sex, with this exception, that they are not to touch those who are marked with the cross. The על for אל before תּחוס is either a slip of the pen, or, as the continued transmission of so striking an error is very improbable, is to be accounted for from the change of א into ע, which is so common in Aramaean. The <hi type="italic">Chetib</hi> עיניכם is the unusual form grammatically considered, and the singular, which is more correct, has been substituted as <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>. תּהרגוּ is followed by למשׁחית, to increase the force of the words and show the impossibility of any life being saved. They are to make a commencement at the sanctuary, because it has been desecrated by the worship of idols, and therefore has ceased to be the house of the Lord. To this command the execution is immediately appended; they began with the old men who were before the house, i.e., they began to slay them. האנשׁים הזּקנים are neither the twenty-five priests (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.16">Eze 8:16</reference>) nor the seventy elders (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.11">Eze 8:11</reference>). The latter were not לפני הבּית, but in a chamber by the outer temple gate; whereas לפני הבּית, in front of the temple house, points to the inner court. This locality makes it natural to think of priests, and consequently the lxx rendered ממּקדּשּׁי by ἀπὸ τῶν ἁγίων μου. But the expression אנשׁים זקנים is an unsuitable one for the priests. We have therefore no doubt to think of men advanced in years, who had come into the court possibly to offer sacrifice, and thereby had become liable to the judgment. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.7">Eze 9:7</reference> the command, which was interrupted in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.9.6">Eze 9:6</reference></hi>, is once more resumed. They are to defile the house, i.e., the temple, namely, by filling the courts with slain. It is in this way that we are to connect together, so far as the sense is concerned, the two clauses, “defile...and fill.” This is required by the facts of the case. For those slain “before the house” could only have been slain in the courts, as there was no space between the temple house and the courts in which men could have been found and slain. But לפני cannot be understood as signifying “in the neighbourhood of the temple,” as Kliefoth supposes, for the simple reason that the progressive order of events would thereby be completely destroyed. The angels who were standing before the altar of burnt-offering could not begin their work by going out of the court to smite the sinners who happened to be in the neighbourhood of the temple, and then returning to the court to do the same there, and then again going out into the city to finish their work there. They could only begin by slaying the sinners who happened to be in the courts, and after having defiled the temple by their corpses, by going out into the city to slay all the ungodly there, as is related in the second clause of the verse (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.9.7">Eze 9:7</reference></hi>).
entries.8f66c7d90742b6d87b78a1204ea0a15ea53efa25: <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.8-Ezek.9.11">Eze 9:8-11</reference> <div eID="gen14857" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Intercession of the Prophet, and the Answer of the Lord</title> <div sID="gen14858" type="x-p"/> Eze 9:8. <hi type="italic">And it came to pass when they smote and I remained, I fell upon my face, and carried, and said: Alas! Lord Jehovah, wilt Thou destroy all the remnant of Israel, by pouring out Thy wrath upon Jerusalem?</hi> Eze 9:9. <hi type="italic">And He said to me: The iniquity of the house of Israel and Judah is immeasurably great, and the land is full of blood-guiltiness, and the city full of perversion; for they say Jehovah hath forsaken the land, and Jehovah seeth not.</hi> Eze 9:10. <hi type="italic">So also shall my eye not look with pity, and I will not spare; I will give their way upon their head.</hi> Eze 9:11. <hi type="italic">And, behold, the man clothed in white linen, who had the writing materials on his hip, brought answer, and said: I have done as thou hast commanded me.</hi> - The <hi type="italic">Chetib</hi> נאשׁאר is an incongruous form, composed of participle and imperfect fused into one, and is evidently a copyist’s error. It is not to be altered into אשּׁאר, however (the 1st pers. imperf. <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>.), but to be read as a participle נשׁאר, and taken with כּהכּותם as a continuation of the circumstantial clause. For the words do not mean that Ezekiel alone was left, but that when the angels smote and he was left, i.e., was spared, was not smitten with the rest, he fell on his face, to entreat the Lord for mercy. These words and the prophet’s intercession both apparently presuppose that among the inhabitants of Jerusalem there was no one found who was marked with the sign of the cross, and therefore could be spared. But this is by no means to be regarded as established. For, in the first place, it is not stated that <hi type="italic">all</hi> had been smitten by the angels; and, secondly, the intercession of the prophet simply assumes that, in comparison with the multitude of the slain, the number of those who were marked with the sign of the cross and spared was so small that it escaped the prophet’s eye, and he was afraid that they might all be slain without exception, and the whole of the remnant of the covenant nation be destroyed. The שׁארית of Israel and Judah is the covenant nation in its existing state, when it had been so reduced by the previous judgments of God, that out of the whole of what was once so numerous a people, only a small portion remained in the land. Although God has previously promised that a remnant shall be preserved (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.3-Ezek.5.4">Eze 5:3-4</reference>), He does not renew this promise to the prophet, but begins by holding up the greatness of the iniquity of Israel, which admits of no sparing, but calls for the most merciless punishment, to show him that, according to the strict demand of justice, the whole nation has deserved destruction. מטּה (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.9">Eze 9:9</reference>) is not equivalent to מוהט, oppression (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.9">Isa 58:9</reference>), but signifies perversion of justice; although משׁפּט is not mentioned, since this is also omitted in <reference osisRef="Exod.23.2">Exo 23:2</reference>, where הטּה occurs in the same sense. For <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.9.9">Eze 9:9</reference></hi>, vid., Eze 8:12. For נתתּי 'דּרכּם בר (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.10">Eze 9:10</reference> and Eze 11:21-22, 31), vid., 1Ki 8:32. While God is conversing with the prophet, the seven angels have performed their work; and in <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.11">Eze 9:11</reference> their leader returns to Jehovah with the announcement that His orders have been executed. He does this, not in his own name only, but in that of all the rest. The first act of the judgment is thus shown to the prophet in a figurative representation. The second act follows in the next chapter.  <chapter eID="Ezek.9"/> <div eID="gen14858" type="x-p"/>

Now the manner of that vengeance which was lately mentioned is expressed. Hence the Prophet says, God exclaimed, so that his command reached to the Chaldeans, who were to be executors of his vengeance, and therefore the imperative mood pleases me better, approach ye therefore. Those who consider the tense past say “visitations,” nor can they do otherwise, because no sense can be elicited from the words — to have approached the prefecture of the city. But if we read the imperative mood, the sense agrees very well, approach ye the prefecture: the thing is put for the persons, or the name of the men may be understood, and thus פקדות, phekdoth, may be taken in the genitive case. As to the general meaning, God commands his servants who held authority over the devoted city, to approach, or apply themselves, or be ready to fulfill his work, and let each, says he, have his instrument of destruction: here destruction is taken actively. For God does not mean that the Chaldeans were armed for their own destruction, but for that of the Jews, and the ruin of the city. It follows —
